Realisation, however, is constrained by incomplete modality availability for individual patients, temporal misalignment between data streams, informative missingness, and the frequent absence of prospective evidence that improved prediction alters management decisions or patient outcomes. This narrative review adopts a use-case-centred structure rather than organisation by modality or algorithm. We examine data foundations that emphasise longitudinal surveillance and lesion-level heterogeneity, fusion strategies designed for missing and asynchronous inputs, and architectures that balance predictive performance with mechanistic interpretability. Applications across therapeutic contexts are evaluated with explicit distinction between retrospective discrimination and demonstrated clinical utility. Evidentiary standards for credible progress—external validation, calibration, missing-modality robustness and decision-impact analysis—are defined, together with governance, equity and regulatory considerations for responsible deployment. The analysis indicates that technical capability is advancing, yet translation requires pragmatic modelling under real-world data constraints and systems that augment rather than replace clinical judgement.

title: Deep learning predicts IDH1 mutation status in acute myeloid leukemia from bone marrow smears
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with IDH1 mutations is amenable to targeted therapy, highlighting the need for reliable identification. We developed an attention-based multiple-instance learning model to predict IDH1 mutation status using bone marrow smear whole-slide images from 436 AML patients across four centers in Germany and the US, achieving a mean single pooled ROC-AUC of 0.81. In top tile analysis, model predictions for IDH1 were associated with immature leukemia phenotypes.

title: Landscape and clinical impact of heterogeneous ALK resistance mutations detected by comprehensive genomic profiling in patients with NSCLC
abstract: ALK rearrangements are established drivers in NSCLC predictive of response to ALK-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Tumors inevitably develop resistance to TKIs, but several therapeutic strategies aimed at overcoming secondary ALK resistance mutations have been developed. This study describes the landscape of ALK resistance mutations detected by next-generation sequencing (NGS) performed on 116,288 tissue and 18,660 liquid specimens from patients with NSCLC. ALK -rearranged ( ALK +) samples were queried for secondary ALK mutations (T1151M/R, L1152R, C1156Y, I1171N/T/S/H/V, F1174X, V1180L, R1192P, L1196M, L1198F, G1202X, D1203N, S1206Y, E1210K, G1269A) associated with acquired resistance to 1st-3rd generation ALK TKIs. Secondary ALK resistance mutations were detected in 8.0% (269/3344) of ALK + samples, most frequently G1202R (42.4%), I1171N (14.9%), and L1196M (14.9%). A US-based de-identified EHR-derived clinico-genomic database (CGDB) was also queried to assess the acquired resistance landscape and treatment patterns for patients with specimens collected >30 days after TKI start. Of these, 5/33 (15%) patients received a subsequent ALK TKI contraindicated by their resistance profile, which was associated with a shorter median real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS) vs a non-contraindicated TKI (4.6 vs. 26.4 months, p = 0.09). Off-target resistance alterations were associated with poor rwPFS (2.7 months), suggesting that these represent a poor prognostic subset that may potentially benefit from combination therapy. The diverse landscape of on- and off-target ALK acquired resistance and variability of post-TKI treatment patterns highlight the importance of repeat NGS testing at progression.

title: The promise and limits of patient-reported outcomes in molecular tumor board-guided care: toward a framework for patient-centered precision oncology
abstract: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) capture symptoms, functioning, quality of life, treatment burden and priorities directly from patients. Their integration into Molecular Tumor Board (MTB)-guided care remains limited and particularly challenging, as recommendations often involve off-label therapies, sparse evidence and complex benefit-burden trade-offs. In this perspective, we propose a four-domain framework encompassing measurement, data integration, decision support and governance to guide longitudinal monitoring and patient-centered learning.

title: Single-cell analysis reveals favorable responses of tumor-associated monocytes to bortezomib-based treatment in multiple myeloma
abstract: The bone marrow microenvironment (BME) has a significant effect on bortezomib (BTZ)-based chemotherapy in patients with multiple myeloma (MM). However, how BME components drive effective BTZ-based chemotherapy to facilitate antitumor responses has yet to be fully understood. Using single-cell transcriptome analysis, we discerned a notable increase in the density of tumor-associated IL1B + monocytes (TAMO_IL1B), a CD14 + monocyte subcluster, within the optimal responders (OR) group compared with the suboptimal responders (SOR) group. TAMO_IL1B in the OR group had significantly greater effects on the TGF-β signaling pathway. The ligand–receptor pair (THBS1-SDC1) interaction intensity in the THBS1 signaling pathway between TAMO_IL1B and tumor plasma cells (TPC) in the OR group was significantly greater than that in the SOR group. Furthermore, pseudotime trajectory analysis indicated that TAMO_IL1B predominantly occupied late differentiation stages and was associated with a favorable response within the OR group. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for TAMO_IL1B in shaping antitumor immunity. The THBS1-SDC1 axis may contribute to interactions between monocytes and plasma cells; however, functional validation is required before any therapeutic implications can be drawn.

title: Decoding small cell lung cancer vulnerabilities: the AI pathway to next-gen therapeutics
abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is aggressive, treatment-sensitive, and prone to relapse. This Review evaluates how generative AI, graph neural networks, molecular language and diffusion models, structure-based design, and multimodal learning can exploit SCLC dependencies for small-molecule discovery. It integrates biomarker-guided patient stratification, resistance, combination therapy, medicinal chemistry, pharmacology, safety, manufacturing, and clinical translation, emphasizing benchmarked, uncertainty-aware, prospectively validated design–build–test–learn workflows.

title: AI-HistoPS: decoding proteomic heterogeneity with subtype resolution from histopathology in liver metastases
abstract: Liver metastasis is a lethal manifestation of diverse malignancies, but its molecular heterogeneity is not readily captured by routine histopathology. Proteomic profiling has identified functional states of metastatic lesions, although their histomorphological and tumor microenvironmental correlates remain incompletely understood. Here, we developed AI-HistoPS, a computational pathology framework for inferring proteomics-informed states from H&E-stained whole slide images. AI-HistoPS integrates pathology foundation model representations with agent-mediated multiple instance learning to capture subtype-associated morphological patterns. Using multicentre cohorts of liver metastases from multiple primary tumor types, we evaluated associations between histomorphology and three proteomic liver metastasis subtypes (LMS1-3). These states were associated with differences in tumor architecture, stromal composition, and immune cell distribution. AI-HistoPS showed subtype discrimination in the discovery cohort and was evaluated across external cohorts, demonstrating the feasibility of histology-derived representations for proteomics-informed stratification across heterogeneous clinical settings. Attention-guided analyses identified tissue regions associated with subtype-related morphological and microenvironmental features. Multiplex immunohistochemistry supported spatial associations between histological patterns and subtype-related protein markers. These findings suggest that routine histopathology may provide a lower-cost approach for approximating proteomics-informed stratification of liver metastases. Further validation in larger, more diverse, prospectively collected cohorts is required before clinical implementation or use in prognostic or treatment-related decision-making.

title: A novel TRG-ypT-ypN 3D staging system for locally advanced gastric cancer patients after neoadjuvant therapy: a multicenter real-world study
abstract: The 8th edition AJCC ypTNM system does not consider tumor regression after neoadjuvant therapy (NAT), which may limit the prognostic accuracy in locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC). This multicenter real-world study included 1270 patients who underwent radical gastrectomy after NAT between January 2020 and January 2025 across twelve institutions, including 763 treated with neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT) and 507 treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NCT). The cohort was divided by institution into a training cohort ( n = 843) and a validation cohort ( n = 427). A TRG-ypT-ypN three-dimensional (3D) staging system was developed in the training cohort using a Cartesian coordinate framework and evaluated in the validation cohort. In the overall NAT cohort, the 3-year overall survival rates for 3D stages I, II, IIIA, and IIIB were 91.9%, 78.1%, 54.9%, and 45.8%, respectively. The 3D staging system showed better prognostic performance than ypTNM in the training and validation cohorts, particularly in the NICT subgroup, whereas the NCT subgroup showed only a non-significant improvement trend. For relapse-free survival, the 3D system also demonstrated modestly improved prognostic performance. Overall, the TRG-ypT-ypN 3D staging system may complement ypTNM for postoperative prognostic assessment in LAGC patients undergoing NAT, especially in the NICT subgroup.

title: Protocols for identification and assessment of bioenergetic differences in diverse pediatric cancer specimens
abstract: Metabolism is frequently altered in cancer (e.g. the Warburg effect, the tendency to overuse glycolysis at the expense of oxidative phosphorylation) and both treatment (e.g. chemotherapy) and nutrition can have the potential to differentially influence metabolism in cancer and healthy tissues. Monitoring metabolic dysregulation in cancer specimens and upon treatments is technically challenging particularly for rare, diverse and hardly metabolically characterized tumors such as those derived of pediatric origin, but may have important clinical applications for improved cancer treatment. Here, we defined a set of detailed protocols to examine functional bioenergetics in cells, organoids, organotypic tissue slices and primary samples from biopsies of childhood cancer patients using Seahorse Cell Analyzers. We provided seven application notes as examples to illustrate the possibility of monitoring metabolic heterogeneity and drug responses in 2D and 3D patient samples. We also provided several potential causes and solutions for troubleshooting to improve data consistency and reliability.

title: Integration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveals stromal cell features in breast cancer
abstract: Stromal cells are key components of the breast cancer tumor microenvironment, yet their heterogeneity, spatial organization, and interactions with tumor and immune cells remain incompletely defined. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data from 233,518 non-immune stromal cells across 349 patients with spatial transcriptomic data from 51 patients. This analysis identified 36 fibroblast, endothelial, and mural cell subsets with distinct transcriptional programs, spatial distributions, and functional associations. ABCA8 + lipid-associated fibroblasts were observed at tumor margins, showed predicted interactions with malignant cells, and were associated with exhaustion-associated T-cell phenotypes. CCL19 + inflammatory fibroblasts showed spatial patterns associated with tertiary lymphoid structure formation, whereas tumor-associated pericytes showed predicted interactions with PGF + tip endothelial cells that may be involved in extracellular matrix deposition and vascular remodeling. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution stromal atlas of breast cancer, resolving stromal subtypes, spatial context, and potential intercellular communication. This resource provides a framework for investigating stromal contributions to tumor progression and immune regulation, although further experimental validation is required.

title: MedGenAgent: a closed-loop agent for oncology CT foundation model pretraining
abstract: Oncology computed tomography (CT) foundation models require large, high-quality training datasets. However, the collection and annotation of such data are costly and time-consuming because tumors occur across multiple anatomical regions and have complex three-dimensional (3D) structures. Strict privacy constraints and institutional variation further limit the availability of large-scale oncology CT datasets. Here, we propose MedGenAgent, a closed-loop agent that supports oncology CT foundation model pretraining in data-constrained settings by iteratively constructing a lesion-rich, anatomically balanced 3D pretraining dataset. MedGenAgent incorporates a Specification resolver tool for structured task parsing and a central Orchestrator tool to coordinate the entire closed-loop agent workflow by leveraging both an Execution layer (including the MAISI synthesis model node for 3D oncology CT sample synthesis, the MedGemma vision-language model node for automated quality control, and the foundation model training node) and a Memory store tool for iterative, feedback-driven updates. Through the synergy of these tools, MedGenAgent synthesized 11,159 CT samples and retained 11,000 quality-controlled samples. By first leveraging this synthetic dataset for pretraining and then aligning with real-world data using only 4400 DeepLesion samples, representing 38.37% of the data used for baseline pretraining, the MedGenAgent-pretrained foundation model achieved performance comparable to the full-data baseline across three retrospective downstream tasks: lesion anatomical site classification, nodule malignancy classification, and cross-institutional NSCLC overall survival classification. Furthermore, automated quality control, independent physician assessment, and workflow analysis demonstrated the construction of a quality-controlled synthetic CT dataset while revealing regional variation in sample quality. Together, these results show that MedGenAgent can autonomously construct quality-controlled synthetic CT data that support the competitive performance of oncology CT foundation models when annotated real-world data are limited.
